parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
Electromagnetic radiation of a single constant frequency is incident on a metal surface. This causes an electron to be emitted.

Explain why the maximum kinetic energy of the electron is independent of the intensity of the incident radiation.

markscheme_points.text: • frequency determines energy of photon • intensity determines number of photons (per unit) • intensity does not determine energy of a photon • kinetic energy (of the electron) depends on the energy

hints: Hint 1: Think in the quantum picture - light of a single frequency arrives as identical packets. What property is the same for every single packet when frequency is fixed?
Hint 2: Now think what turning up the intensity actually changes when frequency stays the same. Does it change each packet, or just how many packets arrive per second?
Hint 3: Remember one photon gives all its energy to one electron. Link the leftover energy of the electron to the energy of that single packet.
parts.proper_answer: Photon energy $E = hf$ depends only on frequency $f$. Intensity is proportional to number of photons per unit time, not energy per photon. One photon interacts with one electron, so max $KE = hf - \Phi$ depends only on $f$, independent of intensity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture light as photons**
Think of the beam not as a continuous wave but as a stream of tiny packets called photons. Each photon carries an amount of energy set only by the frequency, $$E = hf$$ where $h$ is the Planck constant. Because the frequency is constant here, every photon has exactly the same energy.

Step 2: **See what intensity really means**
Increasing intensity at constant frequency does not make each photon more energetic. It just sends more identical photons per second onto the surface. So more electrons can be emitted per second, but each interaction is still one identical photon with one electron.

Step 3: **Follow the energy to the electron**
When a photon is absorbed, its whole energy goes to one electron. Part is used to escape the metal (the work function $\Phi$) and the rest becomes kinetic energy. For the most energetic electrons: $$E_{max} = hf - \Phi$$ Since $hf$ is unchanged and $\Phi$ is a property of the metal, $E_{max}$ is unchanged by intensity.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem: Ultraviolet radiation of wavelength $250\text{ nm}$ is incident on the surface of a sheet of zinc. The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons is $1.4\text{ eV}$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: the energy of a photon of the ultraviolet radiation

markscheme_points.text: E = hc / λ or E = hf and c = fλ

hints: Hint 1: You are given a wavelength in nm for light. Start by converting $250\text{ nm}$ to metres and recall which two universal constants link a light wave to the energy of its photons.
Hint 2: Combine wavelength, speed of light and Planck constant to first get the photon energy in joules. Check your powers of ten carefully.
Hint 3: The answer must be in eV, so plan the final conversion using $1\text{ eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the photon energy relation**
For any photon, wave and particle ideas join together. The wave speed gives $c = f\lambda$ and the particle energy gives $E = hf$. Together: $$E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$$ Use $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$, $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $\lambda = 250\text{ nm} = 250 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m} = 2.50 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}$.

Step 2: **Calculate in joules**
Put the numbers in before touching eV: $$E = \frac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3.00 \times 10^{8})}{250 \times 10^{-9}}$$ $$E = 7.96 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$$ This is the energy of one ultraviolet photon.

Step 3: **Convert joules to electronvolts**
An electronvolt is a much more convenient unit here. Divide by the charge of an electron: $$E = \frac{7.96 \times 10^{-19}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}}$$ $$E = 5.0\text{ eV}$$ Keep 2 significant figures to match the data.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: the work function energy of the surface of the zinc.
hints: Hint 1: Think of energy conservation for one photon and one electron - the photon energy is split into escape energy plus leftover kinetic energy.
Hint 2: Rearrange that energy balance to find the escape energy, then substitute your photon energy from (b)(i) and $1.4\text{ eV}$ for the maximum kinetic energy.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Einstein's photoelectric equation**
The photon energy is shared out. The minimum energy needed just to leave the zinc surface is the work function $\Phi$. Any extra becomes maximum kinetic energy: $$E_{max} = \text{photon energy} - \Phi$$

Step 2: **Solve for the work function**
Rearrange and insert values already in eV, so no further conversion is needed: $$\Phi = \text{photon energy} - E_{max}$$ $$\Phi = 5.0 - 1.4 = 3.6\text{ eV}$$
